title: Let's Pick Some Sled Dogs
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. uses researcher Morten Hansen's finding -- that top workplace performers "do less, then obsess" rather than working the most hours -- and the 1911 race to the South Pole to argue for radical focus in teaching practice. He retells how Roald Amundsen beat the better-resourced Robert Scott by obsessing over a single transportation method (sled dogs) for years, apprenticing with Inuit dog-sledders, while Scott spread himself across five backup transportation methods and ended up expert in none of them, slowed by twenty ill-suited ponies. Stuart applies the lesson directly to teachers: rather than trying to be excellent at everything, a teacher should identify one area of practice -- a "sled dog," such as pop-up debate, essay of the week, or a specific instructional routine -- and obsess over it for a defined stretch, deliberately doing everything else at a "good enough" level. The piece closes with two direct reflection questions asking the reader to name their current sled dog and what they're willing to let go of to make room for it.
points: Morten Hansen's research finding that top performers "do less, then obsess" rather than working the most hours reframes focus, not effort volume, as the actual performance lever.

The Amundsen/Scott contrast makes the cost of spreading effort across many backup options concrete: Scott's five transportation methods left him under-expert in all of them, while Amundsen's singular focus on sled dogs (including two winters apprenticing with Inuit dog-sledders) won the race by a month.

The practical takeaway translates directly to classroom practice: pick one "sled dog" -- a single instructional focus like pop-up debate or essay of the week -- and obsess over it for a defined period rather than attempting uniform excellence everywhere.
The piece ends with two actionable reflection questions (what's your sled dog, and what can you let go of at a "good enough" level) that operationalize the metaphor rather than leaving it abstract.
quotes: But what I didn't discuss in that post is that, in lieu of working insane hours, the high performers tended to "do less, then obsess." They weren't trying to be excellent at everything; they were masters at the arts of focusing and satisficing.

The race ended up a blowout — Amundsen's team, with his small team of explorers and sled dogs, reached the Pole a month before Scott's. This was a bit of a shock — after all, Scott's team had dogs, motor sledges, Siberian ponies, skis, and man-hauling methods for moving through the harsh terrain.

Amundsen succeeded… because he concentrated only on dogs and eschewed backup options. During his three-year trip through the Northwest Passage, he had spent two winters apprenticing with the Inuits who had mastered dog sledging.

He couldn't focus on any of them. Rather than venturing to Siberia to secure ponies, Scott sent his aide… but his aide didn't know about ponies — he was a dog expert. So Scott's team ended up with twenty ill-suited ponies, which slowed the team down on their journey to the pole.
But if you and I want to do this kind of work well, we've got to be like Amundsen. We've got to figure out what our sled dogs are and, while we're at work, become super obsessed about sled dogs.

What's your sled dog right now? What area (singular!) of your practice, if you were to obsess over it and it alone for the next three months, do you think would be likely to produce large downstream benefits to you and your students for years to come?
